evidence: M-O s.v. icon, after Tursellinus (1652): sānctārum imāginum cultōrēs
terms.comment: The classical imāgō, a likeness or portrait (Cic.), with the Church’s sānctus; in church plain imāgō will do. In the Orthodox Church icons are venerated: kissed, censed and given a burning lamp. In the West holy images include statues, and “icon” usually means a painting in the Byzantine manner.
Pliny has it once, of figures. Traupman gives it for the icon on a screen, so it is less clear for a holy one.

icon.against: Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked: īcon, ŏnis
icon.html: Greek εἰκών, with omega in the nominative and omicron in the other cases (εἰκόνος), whence the short o of īconis. Traupman 261 prints īcōn, īconis.
